newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Hong Kong's party spirit blossoms in Orchid Lane.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hong Kong's party spirit blossoms in Orchid Lane.

text.p: Yelling over loud music, beers in hand, a Friday night crowd of young professionals packs the L-shaped street of Lan Kwai Fong, where the explosive growth of trendy bars has mirrored Hong Kong's economic transformation.

A growing army of white-collar professionals in their 20s and 30s has turned the cobbled street behind Hong Kong's bustling Central business district into one of the territory's hottest nightspots, similar to London's Soho.
In this one-time flower market -- "Orchid Lane" -- there is no letup in the festive twilight of British colonial rule.

Throbbing music emanates from popular establishments like California, La Dolce Vita or Club 97, from which pub-crawlers spill out onto the streets, winding down after a week on the trading floor, sealing business deals or jetting around Asia.
"It's just a real hangout," said Mary Justice Thomasson, the spokeswoman for popular Lan Kwai Fong nightclub Club 97.
"It's a pretty young, eclectic crowd."
EXPATRIATES DRESSED UP WITH NOWHERE TO GO
The decline of Hong Kong's manufacturing industry in the 1970s and growth of a vibrant service sector attracted many opportunistic Britons, Australians and Americans here.

Many of these young go-getters -- often dubbed FILTH (Failed In London, Try Hong Kong) -- have brushed off any need for impressive qualifications to slip into high-paying jobs with heavy responsibilities.
The investment banking industry was one area that took off in the 1980s, producing a group of affluent professionals, all dressed up and seeking places to have fun.
"In the early 1980s there was nowhere to go. No one went to Wan Chai because it was just girlie bars," said James Osborn, an expatriate who works for investment house ING Barings.
Wan Chai, once Hong Kong's red light district, was made famous by Richard Mason's novel "The World of Suzie Wong" about a prostitute with a heart of gold.

"Over the last three to five years there has been a huge increase in restaurants and bars (in Lan Kwai Fong) and a huge increase in expats," said Osborn. "If you want to go for a proverbial quick drink after work you go to Lan Kwai Fong."
A YOUNG PROFESSIONAL FRATERNITY
Informal but relatively smart, an after-work drink atmosphere reigns during the early evening. "It turns into 'poseville' later," said Osborn.
Among the "posers" is a new generation of up and coming young, local Chinese professionals -- many educated overseas.
"Young Chinese people have spending power. Here people live at home and they have a huge disposable income," said Thomasson.

Richard Feldman, the chairman of the Lan Kwai Fong Association, said 60 to 70 percent of the clients in this heaving yuppie haunt are now Chinese. "The gweilos stand on the street and drink and the Chinese sit down and eat," he said.
"Gweilo" is an old Chinese term, originally scornful, for Europeans, translated as "foreign devil".
In the densely packed bars, people discuss their jobs and trade business cards. "It's a young, professional fraternity," said Karen Osborne, a public relations consultant at Hill & Knowlton.
"There is a great camaraderie for the expat community. It's a friendly environment with all sorts of nationalities in all sorts of jobs -- a good sort of melting pot."
A HOT SPOT FOR LAST MOMENTS OF COLONIAL RULE
Feldman said Lan Kwai Fong should be one of the hottest spots to live out the last moments of colonial rule when Britain hands Hong Kong back to China on midnight of June 30.
"We are anticipating tens of thousands of people. There will be a real festive feeling in the air," he said.
But with the memories still vivid of a New Year's Eve crush that killed 21 people in Lan Kwai Fong in 1992-93, he said, crowd control will be strict in the tiny area.
Feldman predicts 100 restaurants and bars by the year 2000 compared with a current 62.

American-style fitness centres have also been muscling into the scene, successfully breaking into the work-hard, play-hard lifestyles of young professionals. A landmark is the six-storey California Fitness Center, which opened last year.

The trendy district is also spreading into neighbouring Staunton Street, now known as "Soho" - South of Hollywood Road -- and everyone expects the party spirit to go on blossoming after Hong Kong returns to China on July 1.
